clue.text: Grasped the principle of putting curtains up?

definitions.meaning: the idiom for having learned how to do something
a literal reading: having hung the curtain

explanation.surface: Someone finally works out how a curtain rail goes up.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second reading, where 'hang' is taken literally as hanging curtains.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to have mastered a skill, which is what grasping the principle amounts to.

clue.text: Becoming degenerate and attending races

definitions.meaning: an idiom for being in decline or ruin
literally going to greyhound racing, known in Britain as 'the dogs'

explanation.surface: A gambler's life slides downhill as they keep heading off to the track.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'the dogs' is everyday slang for greyhound racing, so going there means attending races.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes deterioration into a worse, debased condition, matching degeneracy.

clue.text: Censure check

definitions.meaning: to ... an item is to mark it as checked on a list

explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to reprimand someone and to mark an item done on a list.

clue.text: No use? Go home upset, being of a similar type

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and jumbled, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A frustrated person, finding no use in staying, heads home upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' signals rearranging the eleven letters of NO USE and GO HOME together.
explanation.definitionFit: Homogeneous things are uniform in kind, all belonging to the same sort or nature.

clue.text: Indicator in support of hard school

indicators.note: in a down entry the supporting piece sits beneath, so the pointer goes under the letter for hard

parts.note: H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
an arrow is a sign that points the way

explanation.surface: A signpost backs up a tough school's reputation.
explanation.walkthrough: HARROW is a famous English public (private fee-paying) school in north-west London.
explanation.definitionFit: Harrow is a well-known English boarding school, so it is an example of a school.

clue.text: Handle short cut holding chap up

indicators.note: one piece holds the other, so the reversed fellow sits inside the shortened word
short means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: to be nicked is to be cut slightly

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word reads bottom to top

parts.note: a chap is a man

explanation.surface: A brief trim encloses a fellow being lifted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short cut' looks like a single phrase for a quick route, but 'short' instructs dropping the last letter of the cut word; 'holding' and 'up' do the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A handle is informal slang for a person's name, especially a nickname or alias.

clue.text: Dismissed heavy defeat with leader gone

indicators.note: the leader is the opening letter, which is removed

parts.note: a rout is a crushing defeat

explanation.surface: A team suffers a thrashing and loses its captain as well.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman who is dismissed is out.
explanation.definitionFit: A batter who is dismissed in cricket or baseball is said to be out.

clue.text: Independent test after end of term must be better

indicators.note: the test word comes after the letter from term
the end of the word term is its final letter

parts.note: to prove is to test, as in proving ground

explanation.surface: A school report: after an independent exam at the end of term, a pupil must do better.
explanation.definitionFit: To improve is to get better or become better, the plain sense of the phrase.

clue.text: Down, as my career ruined the Oscars, perhaps

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked, so the letters are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A depressed star laments that the Academy Awards wrecked their career.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' rearranges the letters of DOWN AS MY CAREER; 'perhaps' marks the Oscars as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oscars are a celebrated annual prize-giving event, an example of such a ceremony.

clue.text: Settler's living with her at last

definitions.note: read as 'Settler is', the 's linking definition to wordplay

parts.note: one's living is one's income

indicators.note: at last picks the final letter of the word her

explanation.surface: A pioneer's livelihood depends on his wife.
explanation.definitionFit: An incomer is a newcomer who has moved in to live somewhere, as a settler does.

clue.text: Tool providing musical touch

parts.note: Cats is the Andrew Lloyd Webber musical
to paw is to touch clumsily

explanation.surface: An instrument that gives a melodious feel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tool' here means a person used by another, not an implement.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat's paw is a dupe or stooge exploited by someone else, a figurative tool.

clue.text: Make a silly mistake ignoring fine mess

indicators.note: ignoring means leaving out the letter for fine

parts.note: to goof is to blunder
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: Someone blunders and shrugs off a sticky situation.
explanation.definitionFit: Goo is a sticky, messy substance, so it can stand for a mess.

clue.text: Rumoured defect attached to new drug on entry level

indicators.note: new means the letters are made into a fresh arrangement
something rumoured is passed by word of mouth, so a word is taken as it is spoken

parts.note: a flaw is a defect

explanation.surface: Talk of a faulty new drug coming onto the market at a basic level.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges DRUG ON into GROUND; FLAW sounds like FLOOR in a non-rhotic British accent. 'attached to' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The ground floor is the storey at street level where one enters a building.

clue.text: Trendy dresser seeing first article under way

indicators.note: in a down entry the later letters sit beneath the word for way

parts.note: a fashion is a way or manner of doing something
first written as 1ST, its 1 read as the letter I
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A trendy dresser sees the first piece in a new line under way.
explanation.walkthrough: First is abbreviated 1ST, and the digit 1 is read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A fashionista follows the latest styles closely, someone who dresses trendily.

clue.text: Abandoned objective hurt feelings

definitions.note: a verb phrase, hurt the feelings of, matching the verb

parts.note: an event called off is abandoned
an end is an aim or objective

explanation.surface: Giving up on a goal left someone upset.
explanation.definitionFit: To offend someone is to upset or wound them, causing resentment.

clue.text: The girl's in second service, dazzling people

indicators.note: the girl is placed in the other letters

parts.note: Mass is a church service
the girl is her

explanation.surface: A woman takes part in a second church service, among striking people.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of girl's is read as 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Smashers is British slang for strikingly attractive or excellent people.

clue.text: Different standard adopted by parliamentary constituency on energy

indicators.note: in a down entry the first part sits on top of the energy letter
something adopted is taken in, so the standard sits inside the constituency

parts.note: a constituency is a seat in Parliament
par is a standard or norm
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: A political candidate's standards differ after being taken on by a constituency.
explanation.definitionFit: Separate things are distinct and apart, which is what different means.

clue.text: Browbeaten after changing the decor?

indicators.note: changing the arrangement of these letters gives a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is bullied after redecorating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing' rearranges THE DECOR; 'after' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To hector someone is to bully or intimidate them, so hectored means bullied.

clue.text: Lively chat about a bishop's complaint

indicators.note: about means the rearranged word goes around the other letters
lively words get jumbled, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: RR is Right Reverend, a bishop's title

explanation.surface: An animated conversation about a bishop's ailment.
explanation.walkthrough: Right Reverend, abbreviated RR, is the formal style of an Anglican bishop; 'Lively' scrambles and 'about' wraps around.
explanation.definitionFit: Catarrh is excess mucus in the nose and throat, a minor medical complaint.

clue.text: Bishop goes in for starter of spicy soup

indicators.note: the bishop letter replaces the opening letter of the word for spicy

parts.note: risqué means slightly indecent, spicy
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A bishop orders a soup for a spicy starter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spicy' looks like a description of soup, but it means RISQUE (saucy), whose R is replaced by B.
explanation.definitionFit: A bisque is a rich, creamy soup, usually made from shellfish such as lobster.

clue.text: Peaceful American gets release from duties

parts.note: peaceful means quiet

explanation.surface: A calm Yank is relieved of responsibilities.
explanation.definitionFit: A quietus is a discharge from obligation or office, originally the release of a debt.

clue.text: There's no end of brown in intense colour

indicators.note: there is no such letter, so it is removed

parts.note: violent means intense, as in a violent storm

indicators.note: end of picks the final letter of the word brown

explanation.surface: A painter's vivid colour contains no brown at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Violet is a bluish-purple hue, so it is one colour.

clue.text: Hate seeing criminal doesn't eat it

indicators.note: criminal suggests something bent out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: It's a crime to dislike food so much you won't eat it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' rearranges the letters of DOESNT EAT IT; 'seeing' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Detestation is intense loathing, so it is a noun synonym of hate.

clue.text: Anger as sacked without protection

indicators.note: the protective outer layer is the first and last letters, which are removed

parts.note: to be fired is to be sacked

explanation.surface: Fury at being dismissed with no job security.
explanation.definitionFit: Ire is a literary word for wrath or fury, synonymous with anger.

clue.text: Primate will have trouble after resistance in Indian state

indicators.note: the inner letters go in the Indian state

parts.note: Goa is a state on India's west coast

indicators.note: trouble comes after the resistance letter

parts.note: R is the symbol for electrical resistance
ill means trouble or misfortune

explanation.surface: An ape faces trouble after meeting resistance in Goa.
explanation.definitionFit: The gorilla is the largest of the great apes, which are primates.

clue.text: Raised objective ignoring a record

indicators.note: in a down entry raised means read upwards, bottom to top
ignoring means the letter a is omitted

parts.note: a goal is an objective

explanation.surface: A target goes up, overlooking a previous record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ignoring' turns GOAL into GOL, which 'Raised' reverses.
explanation.definitionFit: A log is a written record, as in a ship's log or logbook.

clue.text: Country shoot arranged by the French

indicators.note: by means beside, so the two pieces sit side by side

parts.note: le is French for the

indicators.note: arranged means the letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A photo shoot organised by French people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' signals the scramble and 'by' means placed alongside the French article.
explanation.definitionFit: Lesotho is a landlocked kingdom in southern Africa, completely surrounded by South Africa.

clue.text: Alfred was known to be this good at singular times, and novel

parts.words: Alfred was known to be this
parts.note: King Alfred of Wessex is known as Alfred the Great
S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
by means times in multiplication, as in three by four

explanation.surface: A tribute to King Alfred's excellence at unusual moments, plus a book.
explanation.walkthrough: Alfred the Great was a ninth-century English king.
explanation.definitionFit: The Great Gatsby is F. Scott Fitzgerald's 1925 novel of the Jazz Age.
